title: Ananias of Damascus (Acts 9:10–19)
hook: he's afraid of Saul, goes anyway, and calls him brother

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip and the Ethiopian: a chariot, a scroll, and an honest question. Your line was how can I, unless.

Saul on the road to Damascus, the light, the fall, the voice: that's the half of this story painters love. The second half belongs to a man who appears for only a few verses: Ananias, a disciple living in Damascus. He isn't an apostle, he leaves no letters, and he has heard all about Saul, the man who has been dragging believers off to prison. And one day the Lord tells Ananias to go and find him.
screen: `THE FAMOUS HALF: THE ROAD.` → `THE OTHER HALF: ANANIAS.` → `GO AND FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: The instructions are oddly precise. In the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, and go into the street that is called Strait," and seek, in the house of Judas, one named Saul of Tarsus. He's praying, and he's blind. And Ananias does something very human: he argues. Lord, I've heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem, and he's here with authority to arrest everyone who calls on your name. That's not a lack of faith. It's memory. He knows exactly who Saul is. The answer doesn't take the danger away. Go thy way, the Lord says, "for this man is to me a vessel of election," to carry my name before the Gentiles. So Ananias goes. Picture the walk down that street, the knock, the blind man who once came to arrest people like him. And the first two words out of Ananias's mouth, in the Douay-Rheims: "Brother Saul." Not enemy. Not persecutor. Brother. He lays his hands on him, and immediately something like scales falls from Saul's eyes. He sees, he gets up, he is baptized, and he eats. The future apostle Paul is welcomed into the Church by a disciple who appears for only a few verses. Tradition places the street called Straight on the long main street of old Damascus. And Ananias is honored as a saint: a frightened man who knocked anyway.
screen: `THE STREET CALLED STRAIGHT.` · `ANANIAS ARGUES: I KNOW THIS MAN.` · `A VESSEL OF ELECTION.` · `SCALES FALL FROM HIS EYES.` · then, large: `BROTHER SAUL.`

segments.voice: Think of a person you avoid, not someone dangerous, just someone hard: the one who hurt you, the one who intimidates you, the conversation you keep postponing. Notice what your body does when you picture them; Ananias felt that too, and said so out loud. Then imagine your first two words if you went, something like brother, or sister, or friend, and if you pray, tell God plainly what you're afraid of, the way Ananias did.
Brother. The first word Ananias said to Saul, the man he feared, instead of enemy or persecutor. Today's word.
Your line: brother saul. Tomorrow, an upstairs room in Joppa, full of coats. See you then.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Ananias of Damascus as a saint, and they hear this passage at Mass in the Easter season and on the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January 25.

trapdoor: what you thought: the conversion of Paul was a light on the road, and that was all.
what it means: blind and praying, Saul needs a frightened stranger to come, lay hands on him, and call him brother before he sees again.

what a scholar hears: the story is told three times in Acts: by Luke in chapter 9, and by Paul in chapters 22 and 26. Ananias appears in the first two. tradition identifies the street called Straight with the long straight street of old Damascus.

chat.says: Who was Ananias in Saul's story? Wasn't he scared of Saul?
options: Yes, and he told God so. He went anyway, and his first words were: brother Saul.
No, he had never heard of Saul, so he walked in without a second thought.
He was the companion who led blind Saul by the hand into the city.
chat.meaning: Ananias knew Saul's record and argued with the Lord, but he went, laid hands on him, and called him brother. Scales fell from Saul's eyes.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of Acts 9:11 and 9:15 and Douay-Rheims 'Brother Saul' (9:17).
Ananias honored as a saint (Roman Martyrology, traditionally January 25); confirm.
Acts 9 is read at weekday Mass in the third week of Easter, and Acts 22:3–16 or 9:1–22 on January 25; confirm the howItsDone wording.
The Straight Street (Via Recta) of Damascus 'still there': standard, but confirm phrasing.
Ananias appears in Paul's retellings in Acts 22 but not Acts 26; confirm the trapdoor line.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: Acts 9:11 and 9:15 were quoted from the KJV on the Catholic path; now the Douay-Rheims, verified ('the street that is called Strait', 'a vessel of election'); screen and match follow. Cut 'everyone knows', 'what most of us would do' and 'a man whose name most people have never heard'; Straight Street's location now attributed to tradition.
